title: Blackouts Hit Indian Factories as Coal Crunch Squeezes the Economy
excerpt: Punjab factories face unscheduled 3–4 hour power cuts as coal stocks hit their lowest since 2021 — but the government says depletion has slowed sharply in October and supplies are stabilizing.
body:
• Factories are losing power. In Punjab, homes and industries are enduring lengthy blackouts, and a Ludhiana steel-wire plant owner reports unscheduled 3–4 hour power cuts that force expensive generator use and raise safety risks on the factory floor.
  • The grid is straining nationwide. India faced an average electricity shortfall of nearly 4 GW a day in the first 10 days of October — enough to power about two million rural households — and as of October 4, some 69 power stations, over 40% of the coal-fired fleet, had fuel for just four days or less, the lowest since December 2021.
  • The government says the bleeding is slowing. The Ministry of Coal stated on October 12 that stocks have held above 18 million tonnes since September 29, and the pace of depletion eased sharply: September burned through 7.28 MT (0.24 MT/day), while the first ten days of October lost only 0.56 MT (0.06 MT/day), as coal supplies broadly kept pace with consumption.
  • Captive power plants are the hardest hit. Companies generating their own coal-fired electricity face 94% average premiums at Coal India spot auctions and months-long waits for rail transport — pushing smaller firms to cut output.

Opening: blackouts on the factory floor

In Ludhiana, one of Punjab's biggest industrial cities, Badish Jindal's steel wire plant keeps going dark. Frequent 3–4 hour power cuts force the factory onto expensive backup generators, driving up energy costs while unscheduled stoppages disrupt production schedules, product quality — and safety.

https://x.com/EconomicTimes/status/2109556357548610003

"The power cuts are unscheduled. That makes it difficult to plan our operations and deliveries and affects product quality."

— Badish Jindal, steel wire plant owner, Ludhiana

Homes and industries across Punjab are enduring lengthy blackouts, and Grid Controller of India data show the national grid running an average shortfall of nearly 4 GW a day in the first 10 days of October — enough to power about two million rural households. India generates nearly 70% of its electricity from coal, and coal is running short.

Context & Background: how the crunch built up

The shortage has been months in the making. A late monsoon burst last month in eastern India's coal-mining regions crimped production and hampered rail transport, while unusually warm temperatures kept demand for cooling, irrigation, and industry strong well into October. Chronic rail bottlenecks forced power plants to dip deep into inventories.

By October 4, about 69 power stations — over two-fifths of the nation's coal fleet — had fuel for four days or less, the lowest since December 2021. Auction premiums at Coal India spot sales jumped to 94% over base price in September from 59% in August, with two subsidiaries charging more than 200%.

Impact & Analysis: who pays the price

The pain is uneven: captive power producers — steel, cement, and manufacturing firms generating their own coal-fired electricity — are at a major disadvantage, says Rajiv Agarwal, secretary general of the Indian Captive Power Producers Association. They pay steep auction premiums, buy expensive grid power, and wait months for coal rail transport — forcing smaller firms to cut output.

Power bills have risen in most states on rising coal prices and grid upgrades, and analysts warn sustained shortages could dent manufacturing output — a sector contributing about 14.4% of India's GDP, making industrial blackouts a national growth risk.

The government says the drawdown is easing

New Delhi says the worst of the drawdown is over. In an October 12 statement, the Ministry of Coal said stocks at domestic coal-based plants have held above 18 million tonnes since September 29 — 18.205 MT on October 10 versus 18.932 MT on September 29. The depletion pace has eased sharply: September burned 7.28 MT (0.24 MT/day); the first ten days of October lost only 0.56 MT (0.06 MT/day).

The ministry credits higher rake loading — 469 rakes per day in early October, up 10% from September's 426 — lifting daily supply to 2.49 MT from 2.21 MT, above the 2.37 MT plan on nine of ten days. Stocks even grew on October 2 and 10, and critically low-stock plants are getting redistributed coal.

Diaspora Angle

For NRIs with family in Punjab, these blackouts are personal, not abstract statistics. For diaspora investors, the read is two-sided: factory-floor pain is real, but the October numbers suggest the supply response is gaining traction. The test is whether easing depletion holds through the festival season, when demand typically surges.

What's Next

Two trends are racing: depleted inventories and high auction premiums against rising rake loadings and slowing depletion. If the October improvement holds, India may have avoided a repeat of December 2021. Watch the ministry's weekly figures — and whether Punjab's unscheduled cuts end — for the real verdict.

Sources: Mining Weekly (Bloomberg), The Hindu BusinessLine, The Hindu BusinessLine (Ministry of Coal statement).
